topics.title: The third declension: consonant stems
topics.intro: The third declension is the biggest noun family: φύλαξ (guard), γίγας (giant), ἀγών (contest), ῥήτωρ (speaker), παῖς (child), Ἕλλην (a Greek). The nominative can look odd, so always learn the genitive too: take off -ος and you have the stem. After that the endings are regular: singular -α, -ος, -ι; plural -ες, -ας, -ων, -σι(ν).
topics.teach: Explain how to find the stem of a third-declension noun, using φύλαξ, φύλακος.
topics.talk: Ask {him} to decline ἀγών aloud, singular and plural, and to name an English word that comes from it.
topics.hook: Genitive minus **-ος** = the stem; then add **-α, -ος, -ι** and **-ες, -ας, -ων, -σι(ν)**.

topics.title: The third declension: σῶμα, πόλις, βασιλεύς and family words
topics.intro: Three more patterns. Neuters ending -μα have a stem in -ματ- (σῶμα, σώματος). πόλις (city) and βασιλεύς (king) change their stem vowel. Family words such as πατήρ (father), μήτηρ (mother) and ἀνήρ (man) drop a vowel in some cases, and γυνή (woman) uses a stem γυναικ-.
topics.teach: Explain why τὰ σώματα could be either the subject or the object.
topics.talk: Ask {him} which English words come from σῶμα, πόλις and γυνή.
topics.hook: **-μα** neuters hide a **τ**: σῶμα, σώματος; ὄνομα, ὀνόματος.

topics.title: Pronouns: I, you, we, and αὐτός
topics.intro: Personal pronouns: ἐγώ (I), σύ (you), ἡμεῖς (we), ὑμεῖς (you all). Greek uses ἐγώ or σύ as a subject only for emphasis, because the verb ending already says who. The busy word αὐτός has three jobs: “him, her, it, them” on its own; “-self” next to a noun (αὐτὸς ὁ βασιλεύς, the king himself); and “the same” after the article (ὁ αὐτὸς βασιλεύς, the same king).
topics.teach: Explain the three meanings of αὐτός, with an example of each.
topics.talk: Ask {him} the difference between αὐτὸς ὁ βασιλεύς and ὁ αὐτὸς βασιλεύς.
topics.hook: **αὐτός** has three jobs: alone = him; outside the article = self; inside it = same.

topics.title: This, that, and who: οὗτος, ἐκεῖνος and the relative
topics.intro: οὗτος (this) and ἐκεῖνος (that) stand outside the article: οὗτος ὁ ἀνήρ or ὁ ἀνὴρ οὗτος, “this man”. The relative pronoun ὅς, ἥ, ὅ means “who” or “which”: it takes its gender and number from the noun it refers to, but its case from its own clause.
topics.teach: Explain why the relative in ὁ ἀνὴρ ὃν ὁρῶ is accusative.
topics.talk: Ask {him} to translate “this girl” and “that city” into Greek.
topics.hook: This and that stand outside the article: **οὗτος ὁ ἀνήρ**, this man.

topics.title: Comparison: wiser, wisest
topics.intro: Comparatives (“wiser”) and superlatives (“wisest”) usually add -τερος and -τατος: σοφός, σοφώτερος, σοφώτατος. The commonest adjectives are irregular, just as in English (good, better, best): ἀγαθός, ἀμείνων, ἄριστος. “Than” is ἤ, or the genitive on its own.
topics.teach: Explain two ways of saying “than” in Greek.

topics.title: The weak aorist and the augment
topics.intro: The aorist is the storytelling tense: a single action in the past. The weak (first) aorist adds the augment ἐ- at the front and -σα at the end: ἔλυσα, ἔλυσας, ἔλυσε(ν), ἐλύσαμεν, ἐλύσατε, ἔλυσαν. A verb starting with a vowel lengthens it instead (ἀκούω → ἤκουσα), and a compound verb puts the augment after its prefix (ἀποπέμπω → ἀπέπεμψα).
topics.teach: Explain how to tell ἐπαίδευε (imperfect) from ἐπαίδευσε (aorist).
topics.talk: Ask {him} to tell you the aorist of λύω, all six persons.
topics.hook: Augment at the front, **σα** at the back: ἔλυσα, I freed.

topics.title: Strong and irregular aorists
topics.intro: Many of the commonest verbs have a strong (second) aorist: a different stem with imperfect-style endings. φεύγω → ἔφυγον (I fled), λαμβάνω → ἔλαβον (I took), μανθάνω → ἔμαθον (I learned). A few must simply be learned as new words: λέγω → εἶπον, ὁράω → εἶδον, ἔρχομαι → ἦλθον.
topics.teach: Explain how to tell ἔφευγον from ἔφυγον.
topics.talk: Ask {him} for the aorists of λέγω, ὁράω and ἔρχομαι.
topics.hook: Strong aorists swap the stem, not the endings, like English run and ran: φεύγω → ἔφυγον.

topics.title: Infinitives and commands
topics.intro: The infinitive (“to free”) has a present form, λύειν, and an aorist form, λῦσαι (strong aorists: λαβεῖν, φυγεῖν). Both mean “to…”; the aorist just treats the action as a single event. Commands use the imperative: λῦε! (to one person), λύετε! (to several); aorist λῦσον!, λύσατε! To say “don’t”, use μή.
topics.teach: Explain the difference between λύσατε! and ἐλύσατε.
topics.talk: Ask {him} to give you a command in Greek, and then tell you not to do it.
topics.hook: The augment is for past statements only: λῦσαι (to free) and λῦσον (free!) have none.

topics.title: Contracted verbs: φιλέω, ποιέω (and a taste of τιμάω)
topics.intro: Verbs like φιλέω (I love) and ποιέω (I make, do) have stems ending in ε, which merges with the ending: φιλέ-ω → φιλῶ, φιλέ-ει → φιλεῖ, φιλέ-ομεν → φιλοῦμεν. The rules: ε + ω = ω, ε + ε = ει, ε + ει = ει, ε + ο = ου, ε + ου = ου. Verbs in -άω, like τιμάω (I honour) and ὁράω (I see), contract to α and ω sounds instead: τιμᾷ, ὁρῶμεν.
topics.talk: Ask {him} what φιλοσοφία has to do with φιλέω.
topics.hook: **ε + ο = ου**, **ε + ε = ει**: φιλέομεν → φιλοῦμεν.

topics.title: The middle and passive
topics.intro: Greek verbs have a third set of endings: λύομαι, λύεται, λυόμεθα, λύεσθε, λύονται. In the present these can be passive (“I am being freed”) or middle (“I free for myself”). Some verbs have only these endings but active meanings, like βούλομαι (I want) and γίγνομαι (I become): these are called deponents. “By” a person is ὑπό + genitive.
topics.teach: Explain what a deponent verb is, with an example.
topics.talk: Ask {him} to translate “the horse is freed by the slave” into Greek.

topics.title: Participles in full
topics.intro: A participle is an adjective made from a verb. The present participle (λύων, λύουσα, λῦον: “freeing”) describes something happening at the same time; the aorist participle (λύσας, λύσασα, λῦσαν: “having freed”) something that happened first. Strong aorists have their own: λαβών (having taken), ἰδών (having seen), ἐλθών (having come). Participles agree with their noun like adjectives, which is how you know who is doing what.
topics.teach: Explain how the case of a participle tells you who is doing the action.
topics.talk: Ask {him} to translate ταῦτα εἰπών, and say why it is “having said”.
topics.hook: Present participle = **while**; aorist participle = **having**: λύων, λύσας.

topics.title: Using the cases: time, means and possession
topics.intro: The cases do more than subject and object. The dative can mean “with” or “by means of” (τῷ ξίφει, with the sword) and “on” a day (τῇ ὑστεραίᾳ, on the next day). The accusative can mean “for” a length of time (δέκα ἔτη, for ten years). The genitive shows possession (ἡ τοῦ βασιλέως θυγάτηρ) and “during” a time (νυκτός, by night). And ὦ + the vocative calls someone: ὦ φίλε!
topics.teach: Explain how Greek says “for ten years” and “on the third day”.
topics.talk: Ask {him} how an Athenian speaker would begin a speech: ὦ ἄνδρες Ἀθηναῖοι.
topics.hook: Time: accusative = how long; dative = when; genitive = within which.

topics.title: Questions and negatives
topics.intro: Greek marks a question with ; (which looks like our semicolon). Many question words begin with π- or τ-: τίς; (who?), τί; (what? why?), ποῦ; (where?), πότε; (when?), πῶς; (how?). ἆρα introduces a yes-or-no question. “Not” is οὐ (οὐκ before a smooth breathing, οὐχ before a rough one) in statements, but μή with commands and infinitives.
topics.teach: Explain when Greek uses μή instead of οὐ.
topics.talk: Ask {him} three questions in Greek: who are you, where are you, why are you running?
topics.hook: π- asks: ποῦ; πότε; πῶς; Then **οὐ** states facts, and **μή** gives orders.

topics.title: Reading: Daedalus and Icarus, Arachne
topics.intro: Two more myths in Greek, mostly in the present tense, with a few new words in the glossary. Read each sentence aloud, find the verb, then the subject.
topics.teach: Explain what οὖν does in “ὁ οὖν Δαίδαλος… πτέρυγας ποιεῖ”.
topics.talk: Ask {him} to retell the Arachne story from Athena’s point of view.
topics.hook: Find the verb, then the subject: Daedalus makes, Icarus flies, the sun melts.

topics.title: Reading: Orpheus, and Heracles and the Hydra
topics.intro: These stories mix the present with the imperfect (ᾖδεν, εἶχεν, ἐφύοντο) and use third-declension nouns and pronouns.
topics.teach: Explain why ἐφύοντο is imperfect, and what that adds to the Hydra story.
topics.talk: Ask {him} why Orpheus looked back. What would {she} have done?
topics.hook: Imperfect = it kept happening: the Hydra’s heads kept growing back.

topics.title: Reading: the Sirens, and Jason and the golden fleece
topics.intro: Real storytelling Greek: weak and strong aorists, infinitives and commands. Watch the front of each verb for the augment.
topics.teach: Explain the difference between κλεῖσον and ἔκλεισεν in the Sirens story.
topics.talk: Ask {him} which of the Argonauts {she} would want on the ship, and why.
topics.hook: Augment = it happened (ἔκλεισεν); no augment = an order or an infinitive (κλεῖσον).

topics.title: Reading: the wooden horse, and Perseus
topics.intro: The hardest reading of the year: participles, comparatives and the genitive absolute, the way Greek historians wrote. Take one clause at a time.
topics.teach: Explain how the participles in the wooden-horse story move the action along.
topics.talk: Ask {him} to find every participle in the Perseus story.
topics.hook: One clause at a time: find the participles, then the main verb.

topics.title: The genitive absolute
topics.intro: A noun and a participle in the genitive, standing apart from the rest of the sentence, set the scene: τῆς νυκτὸς γενομένης, “when night had fallen”; τῶν Γοργόνων καθευδουσῶν, “while the Gorgons were sleeping”. Translate it with “when”, “while”, “after” or “because”.
topics.teach: Explain how to spot a genitive absolute and how to translate it.
topics.talk: Ask {him} to make up an English sentence that starts “While the Cyclops was sleeping…”, then try it in Greek.
topics.hook: Noun + participle, both genitive, set the scene: **τῆς νυκτὸς γενομένης**, when night had fallen.

items.hook: Find the stem from the genitive, then add the endings: φύλαξ, φύλακος → φυλακ-.

items.prompt: Which are the third-declension singular endings for the accusative, genitive and dative?

options.feedback: Those are second declension (λόγον, λόγου, λόγῳ).
Those are first declension (τιμήν, τιμῆς, τιμῇ).

items.explain: φύλαξ, φύλακα, φύλακος, φύλακι. The nominative varies, so learn it with the genitive.
items.hook: Singular -α, -ος, -ι: φύλακα, φύλακος, φύλακι.

items.prompt: Which are the third-declension plural endings (nominative, accusative, genitive, dative)?

options.feedback: Those are second declension.
Those are first declension.

items.explain: φύλακες, φύλακας, φυλάκων, φύλαξι(ν).
items.hook: Plural -ες, -ας, -ων, -σι(ν): φύλακες, φύλακας, φυλάκων, φύλαξι(ν).

items.prompt: γίγας (giant) has the genitive γίγαντος. What is its stem?

options.feedback: Take -ος off the genitive: γίγαντ-ος.
The nominative hides the stem. The genitive shows it.

items.explain: Genitive minus -ος = stem: γίγαντ-ος → γιγαντ-. “Gigantic” keeps the -ντ-.
items.hook: γίγας, γίγαντος: the stem keeps its ντ.
items.example: Gigantic still keeps the -nt- of γιγαντ-.

items.prompt: Why is the dative plural of φύλαξ written φύλαξι(ν), not φύλακσι?

options.feedback: It is perfectly regular: the stem φυλακ- + -σι.

options.text: The ξ shows it is plural
options.feedback: ξ is just how Greek writes κσ.

items.explain: Stem φυλακ- + ending -σι(ν) = φυλακσι → φύλαξι(ν). The same thing happens in the nominative: φυλακ-ς → φύλαξ.
items.hook: κ + σ = ξ, just as in φύλαξ itself.

items.prompt: The dative plural of γίγας (stem γιγαντ-) is γίγασι(ν). What happened?

options.feedback: It is a regular sound change.

options.text: It comes from a different word
options.feedback: Same word: γίγας, γίγαντος.

items.explain: γιγαντ- + σι → γίγασι(ν), and λεοντ- + σι → λέουσι(ν): ντ disappears before σ, and the vowel lengthens.
items.hook: ντ vanishes before σ: γίγασι(ν), λέουσι(ν).

items.prompt: What does **ὁ παῖς** (genitive παιδός) mean?
items.explain: παῖς, παῖδα, παιδός, παιδί: a child (boy or girl). It gives us paediatrics and pedagogy.
items.hook: παῖς, παιδός → **paediatrics**, children’s medicine.

items.prompt: What does **ὁ Ἕλλην** (genitive Ἕλληνος) mean?
items.explain: The Greeks called themselves Ἕλληνες (Hellenes) and their land Ἑλλάς (Hellas).
items.hook: Ἕλλην → **Hellenic**, Greek. Hellas is Greece’s own name for itself.
items.example: Greek stamps still say ΕΛΛΑΣ, Hellas.

items.prompt: What does **ὁ ἀγών** (genitive ἀγῶνος) mean?
items.explain: ἀγών = a contest or struggle: the games at Olympia were ἀγῶνες. English “agony” first meant a struggle.
items.hook: ἀγών → **agony**, **protagonist** and **antagonist**.

items.prompt: Which is the genitive singular of **ὁ ῥήτωρ** (speaker)?

options.feedback: That is the accusative singular.
That is the dative singular.
That is the nominative plural.

items.explain: ῥήτωρ, ῥήτορα, ῥήτορος, ῥήτορι. Rhetoric is the speaker’s art.
items.hook: ῥήτωρ → **rhetoric**, the speaker’s art.

items.prompt: In **οἱ φύλακες τὸν γίγαντα διώκουσιν**, who is chasing whom?

options.text: The guards are chasing the giant
The giant is chasing the guards
options.feedback: γίγαντα is accusative (the object); φύλακες is nominative plural (the subject).

options.text: The guard is chasing the giants
options.feedback: φύλακες is plural and γίγαντα singular.

items.explain: φύλακες: nominative plural, subject. γίγαντα: accusative singular, object. διώκουσιν: they chase.
items.hook: Plural -ες = subject; singular -α = object.

items.prompt: What does **ἡ νύξ, τῆς νυκτός** mean?

options.feedback: A nymph is νύμφη.
An island is νῆσος.

items.explain: νύξ, νύκτα, νυκτός, νυκτί. Nyx was also the goddess of night.
items.hook: νύξ, νυκτός: Nyx was the goddess of night.

items.prompt: Why does φύλαξ become φυλάκων in the genitive plural?

options.text: The long -ων stops the accent staying three syllables back
The genitive plural always moves the accent to the stem
options.feedback: Not always: it moves here only because the ending -ων is long.

options.text: Genitive plurals always take a circumflex on the ending
options.feedback: Third-declension -ων usually has the acute on the syllable before: φυλάκων, ἀγώνων.

items.explain: A noun keeps its accent where it can. With a long last syllable (-ων), it can be no further back than the second-to-last syllable.
items.hook: Long last syllable? Then the accent can go back only two syllables: φυλάκων.
σῶμα, σώματος: the stem σωματ- appears in every case except the nominative and accusative singular and the dative plural σώμασι(ν).

items.prompt: σῶμα (body) has the genitive σώματος. What is its dative singular?

options.feedback: -ᾳ is first declension.
That is the genitive.

items.explain: σῶμα, σῶμα, σώματος, σώματι: stem σωματ- + -ι.
items.hook: σωματ- + ι = σώματι.

items.prompt: Which English words come from **σῶμα, σώματος** (body)?

options.feedback: Those come from Latin and French.
Those are old English words.

items.explain: Psychosomatic: of mind and body. Chromosome: “colour body”, because they show up when stained.
items.hook: σῶμα → psychosomatic (mind and body), chromosome (colour body).

items.prompt: Why can **τὰ σώματα** be either the subject or the object?

options.text: Neuter nouns always have the same nominative and accusative
σώματα is a dative plural that can do both jobs
options.feedback: It is nominative or accusative plural; the dative plural is σώμασι(ν).

options.text: Third-declension nouns have no separate accusative form
options.feedback: They do: φύλακα, γίγαντα.

items.explain: Neuters never tell you subject from object by their ending: use the verb and the other nouns.
items.hook: Neuters: nominative = accusative, always.

items.prompt: What does **τὸ πρᾶγμα** (genitive πράγματος) mean?
items.explain: πρᾶγμα = a thing done, a matter, an affair: “pragmatic” means practical.
items.hook: πρᾶγμα (a thing done) → **pragmatic**, practical.
items.example: A pragmatic person cares about what works, not about theory.

items.prompt: Which is the accusative singular of **ἡ πόλις**?

options.feedback: πόλις takes -ν, not -α, in the accusative singular.
That is the genitive.

items.explain: πόλις, πόλιν, πόλεως, πόλει; plural πόλεις, πόλεις, πόλεων, πόλεσι(ν).
items.hook: πόλις, πόλιν: the accusative takes -ν, like τιμήν.

items.prompt: What does **τῆς πόλεως** mean?

options.feedback: That would be the dative, τῇ πόλει.
That would be αἱ πόλεις.

items.explain: πόλεως is the genitive singular: of the city. A metropolis is a “mother city”.
items.hook: πόλεως, of the city: a **metropolis** is a mother city.

items.prompt: What is the genitive singular of **ὁ βασιλεύς** (king)?

options.feedback: The second-declension -ου does not apply here.
That is the dative.

items.explain: βασιλεύς, βασιλέα, βασιλέως, βασιλεῖ. Θησεύς, Ὀδυσσεύς and Περσεύς decline the same way.
items.hook: βασιλεύς, βασιλέως → **basilica**, a royal hall.

items.prompt: In the Theseus story, why is it **τὸν Θησέα**, not τὸν Θησεύν?

options.text: It is a poetic form that Homer uses
options.feedback: It is the ordinary prose form, like βασιλέα.

options.text: Θησέα is the accusative plural of Θησεύς
options.feedback: τόν is singular.

items.explain: βασιλεύς → βασιλέα; Θησεύς → Θησέα; Περσεύς → Περσέα.
items.hook: The βασιλεύς family: Θησεύς, Ὀδυσσεύς and Περσεύς all go -έα, -έως, -εῖ.

items.prompt: ὁ πατήρ (father) has the genitive πατρός. What does **τοῦ πατρός** mean?

options.feedback: That would be τῷ πατρί.
That would be οἱ πατέρες.

items.explain: πατήρ, πατέρα, πατρός, πατρί: the ε drops out in the genitive and dative singular.
items.hook: πατήρ, πατρός → πατρίς, the fatherland, and so **patriot**.

items.prompt: Which is the dative plural of **ὁ ἀνήρ** (man)?

options.feedback: -οις is second declension.
That is the nominative plural.

items.explain: ἀνήρ, ἄνδρα, ἀνδρός, ἀνδρί; ἄνδρες, ἄνδρας, ἀνδρῶν, ἀνδράσι(ν).
items.hook: ἀνδράσι(ν): an α slips in to make ἀνδρ- + σι sayable.

items.prompt: What is unusual about **ἡ γυνή** (woman)?

options.text: Its other cases use the stem γυναικ-
It is masculine, despite meaning woman
options.feedback: It is feminine: ἡ γυνή.

options.text: It has no plural form at all
options.feedback: The plural is γυναῖκες.

items.explain: γυνή is irregular. “Gynaecology” comes from the stem γυναικ-.
items.hook: γυναικ- → **gynaecology**.

items.prompt: The king of the gods declines oddly. Which is the accusative of **Ζεύς**?

options.feedback: There is no such form.
That is the genitive: of Zeus.

items.explain: Ζεύς, Δία, Διός, Διί; and when you call him, ὦ Ζεῦ.
items.hook: Ζεύς, Δία, Διός, Διί. Ζεῦ πάτερ, “father Zeus”, is a cousin of Latin Jupiter.

items.prompt: What does **με** mean in **ὁ Κύκλωψ με διώκει**?

options.feedback: I is ἐγώ, the nominative. με is accusative.
My (of me) would be μου.

items.explain: ἐγώ, ἐμέ (με), ἐμοῦ (μου), ἐμοί (μοι): I, me, of me, to me.
items.hook: ἐγώ, ἐμέ, ἐμοῦ, ἐμοί: me hides inside ἐμέ.

items.prompt: Why is ἐγώ often left out of a Greek sentence?

options.text: It is thought rude to say “I” in Greek
options.feedback: Not rude: just unnecessary.
It appears whenever the speaker wants to stress “I”.

items.explain: λύω already means “I free”. ἐγὼ λύω = “I (and not you) am freeing”.
items.hook: ἐγώ, a cousin of Latin **ego**, is added only for emphasis: the verb ending already says “I”.

items.prompt: What does **ἡμεῖς** mean?
items.explain: ἡμεῖς, ἡμᾶς, ἡμῶν, ἡμῖν: we, us, of us, to us.
items.hook: Chant: ἡμεῖς, ἡμᾶς, ἡμῶν, ἡμῖν: we, us, of us, to us.

items.prompt: What does **ὑμῖν** mean?
items.explain: ὑμεῖς, ὑμᾶς, ὑμῶν, ὑμῖν: you, you, of you, to you (all plural).
items.hook: -ῖν = to: ὑμῖν, to you; ἡμῖν, to us.

items.prompt: Which is the accusative of **σύ** (you, singular)?

options.feedback: σοί is the dative: to you.
σοῦ is the genitive: of you.

items.explain: σύ, σέ, σοῦ, σοί.
items.hook: σύ, σέ, σοῦ, σοί: like old English thou, thee.

items.prompt: In **ὁ στρατηγὸς αὐτὸν ὁρᾷ** (ὁρᾷ = sees), what does αὐτόν mean?

options.feedback: αὐτός means “-self” only next to a noun or as an emphatic subject. On its own in the accusative it means “him”.
“The same man” needs the article: τὸν αὐτόν.

items.explain: Use 1 of αὐτός: on its own, not in the nominative, it means him, her, it or them.
items.hook: αὐτόν on its own = him.

items.prompt: **αὐτὸς ὁ βασιλεύς** means…

options.feedback: The same king is ὁ αὐτὸς βασιλεύς, with the article first.
His king would be ὁ βασιλεὺς αὐτοῦ.

items.explain: Use 2 of αὐτός: outside the article it means “-self”.
items.hook: αὐτὸς ὁ βασιλεύς: outside the article sandwich = self.

items.prompt: **ὁ αὐτὸς βασιλεύς** means…

options.feedback: That is αὐτὸς ὁ βασιλεύς.
Alone would be μόνος.

items.explain: Use 3 of αὐτός: inside the article (ὁ αὐτός) it means “the same”.
items.hook: ὁ αὐτός: inside the article sandwich = same.

items.prompt: In **τὰ ἔργα αὐτῆς θαυμάζουσιν**, what does αὐτῆς mean?

options.text: herself: she herself admires the works
options.feedback: On its own in the genitive, αὐτῆς means “of her”.

options.text: the same: they admire the same works
options.feedback: “The same” needs the article.

items.explain: αὐτοῦ = his, αὐτῆς = her, αὐτῶν = their (literally of him, of her, of them).
items.hook: αὐτοῦ his, αὐτῆς her, αὐτῶν their.

items.prompt: **αὐτοὶ φεύγομεν** means…

options.feedback: φεύγομεν is “we”; αὐτοί adds “ourselves”.
That would be φεύγομεν αὐτούς.

items.explain: In the nominative, αὐτός emphasises the subject: αὐτοὶ φεύγομεν, we flee by ourselves.
items.hook: αὐτός in the nominative stresses the subject: we ourselves.

items.prompt: Put the forms of ἐγώ in case order: nominative, accusative, genitive, dative.
items.explain: ἐγώ (I), ἐμέ (me), ἐμοῦ (of me), ἐμοί (to me).
items.hook: Case order: nominative, accusative, genitive, dative: ἐγώ, ἐμέ, ἐμοῦ, ἐμοί.

items.prompt: Which word means “us”?

options.feedback: ἡμεῖς is the nominative: we.
ὑμᾶς is “you” (plural).

items.explain: ἡμεῖς, ἡμᾶς, ἡμῶν, ἡμῖν. The υ/η difference matters: ὑμεῖς is “you”.
items.hook: ἡμᾶς us, ὑμᾶς you: η for us, υ for you.

items.prompt: What does **οὗτος ὁ ἀνήρ** mean?

options.feedback: That man is ἐκεῖνος ὁ ἀνήρ.
“Such a man” would be τοιοῦτος ἀνήρ.

items.explain: οὗτος stands outside the article: οὗτος ὁ ἀνήρ or ὁ ἀνὴρ οὗτος, this man.
items.hook: οὗτος ὁ ἀνήρ: this man, with οὗτος outside the article.

items.prompt: What does **ἐκείνη ἡ κόρη** mean?

options.feedback: This girl is αὕτη ἡ κόρη.
Her girl would be ἡ κόρη αὐτῆς.

items.explain: ἐκεῖνος, ἐκείνη, ἐκεῖνο: that.
items.hook: ἐκεῖ = there: ἐκείνη, that one over there.

items.prompt: Which form of οὗτος goes with **τὴν ναῦν** (the ship, feminine accusative)?

options.feedback: τοῦτον is masculine.
τοῦτο is neuter.

items.explain: ταύτην τὴν ναῦν, this ship. οὗτος, αὕτη, τοῦτο; accusative τοῦτον, ταύτην, τοῦτο.
items.hook: ταύτην τὴν ναῦν: both end -ην.

items.prompt: What does **ταῦτα** mean?

options.feedback: This man is οὗτος.
Those women would be ἐκεῖναι.

items.explain: ταῦτα is neuter plural: these things. Greek often uses it for “this” about something just said.
items.hook: ταῦτα: these things, often “this” about what has just been said.

items.prompt: What does **ταῦτα εἰπών** mean at the start of a sentence?
items.explain: εἰπών is the aorist participle of λέγω: “having said this”, a favourite way to move a story on.
items.hook: ταῦτα εἰπών: the storyteller’s “having said this”.

items.prompt: Which word means “that” (masculine, nominative)?

options.feedback: οὗτος means this.
αὐτός means him, -self or the same.

items.explain: οὗτος = this (near), ἐκεῖνος = that (further away).
items.hook: οὗτος near, ἐκεῖνος far.

items.prompt: In **ὁ ἀνὴρ ὃν ὁρῶ στρατηγός ἐστιν** (ὁρῶ = I see), why is the relative ὅν accusative?

options.text: It is the object of ὁρῶ in its own clause

options.feedback: ὁ ἀνήρ is nominative. The relative takes its case from its own clause.

options.text: Relative pronouns are always in the accusative
options.feedback: They can be any case.

items.explain: “The man whom I see is a general.” Gender and number from ὁ ἀνήρ (masculine singular); case from ὁρῶ (object).
items.hook: The relative: gender and number from its noun, case from its own clause.

items.prompt: Translate **ἡ κόρη ἣ ᾄδει καλή ἐστιν**.

options.text: The girl who is singing is beautiful.

options.feedback: ἣ ᾄδει is a relative clause: “who is singing”. The main verb is ἐστιν.

options.text: The girl sings to the beautiful woman.
options.feedback: There is no second woman.

items.explain: ἥ is the relative (feminine nominative): who. In running text its accent turns grave: ἣ.
items.hook: ἣ ᾄδει: who is singing. ᾄδω (I sing) is the verb behind **ode**.

items.prompt: Which relative goes with **τὰ δῶρα** as the subject of its clause (“the gifts which…”)?

options.feedback: ἅς is feminine accusative plural.
οἵ is masculine plural.

items.explain: Neuter plural nominative: ἅ. τὰ δῶρα ἃ ἐκεῖ ἐστιν = the gifts which are there.
items.hook: The neuter plural relative ἅ looks like the article τά without its τ.

items.prompt: How do you tell **ἡ** (the, feminine) from **ἥ** (who, feminine)?

options.text: The article ἡ has no accent; the relative ἥ has one
They are the same word, written two ways
options.feedback: Same letters, different words: the accent tells them apart.

options.text: ἥ is the plural form of the article ἡ
options.feedback: Both are singular.

items.explain: ὁ, ἡ, οἱ, αἱ have no accent. The relatives ὅς, ἥ, οἵ, αἵ always do.
items.hook: Article: no accent. Relative: an accent and a rough breathing.

items.prompt: Translate **οὗτοι οἱ στρατιῶται ἐκεῖνον τὸν ποταμὸν φυλάσσουσιν**.

options.feedback: οὗτοι = these; ἐκεῖνον = that.
οἱ στρατιῶται (nominative) are the subject.

items.explain: οὗτοι οἱ στρατιῶται: these soldiers. ἐκεῖνον τὸν ποταμόν: that river. φυλάσσουσιν: they guard.
items.hook: οὗτοι these, ἐκεῖνον that.

items.prompt: What does **σοφώτερος** mean?

options.feedback: Wisest is σοφώτατος.
Wisdom is σοφία.

items.explain: σοφός, σοφώτερος, σοφώτατος: wise, wiser, wisest.
items.hook: -τερος = -er: σοφώτερος, wiser.

items.prompt: What does **σοφώτατος** mean?

options.feedback: Wiser is σοφώτερος.
Greek uses the superlative for “very”, not “too”.

items.explain: The superlative can mean “the most…” or just “very…”.
items.hook: -τατος = -est: σοφώτατος, wisest.

items.prompt: Why is it σοφώτερος but δεινότερος?

options.text: A short syllable before it lengthens ο to ω

options.feedback: Both are regular.

options.text: It is a spelling choice that varies by author
options.feedback: It is a rule.

items.explain: σο- is short, so σοφώτερος (also νεώτερος); δει- is long, so δεινότερος (also μικρότερος).
items.hook: Short syllable before it → ω: σοφώτερος, νεώτερος.

items.prompt: What does **ἀμείνων** mean?

options.feedback: Best is ἄριστος.
Worse is κακίων.

items.explain: ἀγαθός, ἀμείνων, ἄριστος: good, better, best.
items.hook: Good, better, best: ἀγαθός, ἀμείνων, ἄριστος.

items.prompt: Which is the superlative of **μέγας** (big)?

options.feedback: μείζων is the comparative: bigger.
μεγάλη is the feminine of μέγας.

items.explain: μέγας, μείζων, μέγιστος: big, bigger, biggest. The Cyclops was μέγιστος.
items.hook: μέγας, μείζων, μέγιστος: big, bigger, biggest.

items.prompt: Which English word comes from **ἄριστος** (best) + κράτος (power)?
items.explain: Aristocracy: rule by the best (or by those who think they are).
items.hook: ἄριστος + κράτος = aristocracy, rule by the best.

items.prompt: Translate **ὁ Ἀχιλλεὺς ἀνδρειότερός ἐστι τοῦ Ἕκτορος**.

options.feedback: τοῦ Ἕκτορος is genitive: “than Hector”.
ἀνδρειότερος is comparative: braver.

items.explain: The genitive on its own can mean “than”: τοῦ Ἕκτορος, than Hector.
items.hook: The genitive alone can mean than: τοῦ Ἕκτορος, than Hector.

items.prompt: Translate **ἡ Ἀθηνᾶ σοφωτέρα ἐστὶν ἢ ὁ Ἄρης**.

options.feedback: The comparative goes with ἡ Ἀθηνᾶ; ἤ (than) introduces Ares.
σοφωτέρα is comparative: wiser.

items.explain: ἤ = than, with both people in the same case.
items.hook: ἤ = than, with the same case on both sides.

items.prompt: What does **ὡς τάχιστα** mean?

options.feedback: τάχιστα is from ταχύς, quick.
Faster is θᾶττον.

items.explain: ὡς + superlative = as … as possible: ὡς τάχιστα, as fast as possible.
items.hook: ὡς + superlative = as … as possible.

items.prompt: Which is the comparative of **κακός** (bad)?

options.feedback: κακός is irregular.
κάκιστος is the superlative: worst.

items.explain: κακός, κακίων, κάκιστος: bad, worse, worst.
items.hook: κακός, κακίων, κάκιστος: bad, worse, worst.

items.prompt: What does **οἱ πλεῖστοι τῶν στρατιωτῶν** mean?
items.explain: πολύς, πλείων, πλεῖστος: much, more, most.
items.hook: πολύς, πλείων, πλεῖστος: much, more, most.
items.example: The Pleistocene, the age of the mammoths, is named “most new”: πλεῖστος + καινός.

items.prompt: In Arachne’s boast **ἐγὼ κάλλιον ὑφαίνω ἢ ἡ Ἀθηνᾶ**, what does κάλλιον mean?

options.feedback: Most beautifully would be κάλλιστα.
Beautiful is καλός.

items.explain: The neuter comparative works as an adverb: κάλλιον, more beautifully. καλός, καλλίων, κάλλιστος.
items.hook: καλός, καλλίων, κάλλιστος: calligraphy is beautiful writing.
Augment + stem + σα: ἐ-λυ-σα, I freed.

items.prompt: Put the weak aorist of λύω in order: I, you (sg), he, we, you (pl), they.
items.explain: ἔλυσα, ἔλυσας, ἔλυσε(ν), ἐλύσαμεν, ἐλύσατε, ἔλυσαν: I freed… they freed.
items.hook: Chant: ἔλυσα, ἔλυσας, ἔλυσε(ν), ἐλύσαμεν, ἐλύσατε, ἔλυσαν.

items.prompt: What is the aorist of **ἀκούω** (I hear), “I heard”?

options.feedback: A verb starting with a vowel lengthens it instead of adding ἐ-: α → η.
That has no augment: it looks like a future.

items.explain: Augment on a vowel: α → η, ε → η, ο → ω. ἀκούω → ἤκουσα.
items.hook: Vowel verbs lengthen instead: α → η, ἀκούω → ἤκουσα.

items.prompt: What is the aorist of **ἀποπέμπω** (I send away), “I sent away”?

options.feedback: The augment goes after the prefix, not before it.
That is the future: no augment.

items.explain: ἀπο- + ἐ + πεμψα → ἀπέπεμψα (the ο of ἀπο- drops out before the ε).
items.hook: A compound puts the augment after its prefix: ἀπ-έ-πεμψα.

items.prompt: Why is the aorist of γράφω written **ἔγραψα**?

options.feedback: It is regular: ἐ + γραφ + σα.

options.text: ψ is the sign of the past
options.feedback: The augment shows the past; ψ is just φ + σ.

items.explain: π, β, φ + σ → ψ (ἔπεμψα, ἔγραψα); κ, γ, χ + σ → ξ (ἐδίωξα).
items.hook: φ + σ = ψ: ἔγραψα.

items.prompt: What does **ἐδίωξαν** mean?

options.feedback: They were chasing is ἐδίωκον.
The augment ἐ- shows a past tense.

items.explain: ἐ- + διωκ + σαν → ἐδίωξαν (κ + σ = ξ): they chased.
items.hook: κ + σ = ξ: ἐδίωξαν.

items.prompt: What is the difference between **ἐπαίδευε** and **ἐπαίδευσε**?

options.text: ἐπαίδευε = he was teaching; ἐπαίδευσε = he taught
ἐπαίδευε = he taught; ἐπαίδευσε = he was teaching
options.feedback: The σ marks the aorist: one finished action.

options.text: ἐπαίδευσε is the future: he will teach
options.feedback: The augment shows it is past.

items.explain: Imperfect: a continuing action. Aorist: a single, completed action.
items.hook: σ = a snapshot (aorist); no σ = a film (imperfect).

items.prompt: Which form means “he ordered” (from κελεύω)?

options.feedback: κελεύσει is the future: he will order.
ἐκέλευε(ν) is the imperfect: he was ordering.

items.explain: ἐ- + κελευ + σε: ἐκέλευσε(ν), he ordered.
items.hook: ἐ- + κελευ + σε: ἐκέλευσε(ν), he ordered.

items.prompt: What does **ἐποίησε(ν)** (from ποιέω, I make) mean?

options.feedback: He makes is ποιεῖ.
He was making is ἐποίει.

items.explain: Contracted verbs lengthen the stem vowel before the σ: ποιε- → ποιησα. ἐποίησε(ν), he made.
items.hook: ε lengthens to η before the σ: ἐποίησε(ν).

items.prompt: What happens to the augment of a verb that begins with **ε**, like ἐθέλω?

options.text: The ε lengthens to η: ἤθελον (I was wishing)
The ε doubles: εεθελον (I was wishing)
options.feedback: Greek lengthens the vowel instead.

options.text: The ε becomes ει: εἴθελον (I was wishing)
options.feedback: ἐθέλω augments to η, not ει: ἤθελον. (A few verbs, like ἔχω → εἶχον, do use ει.)

items.explain: ε → η: ἐθέλω, ἤθελον. Odysseus ἤθελε τῶν Σειρήνων ἀκούειν.
items.hook: ε → η: ἐθέλω, ἤθελον.

items.prompt: Which is the aorist of **πιστεύω**, “I trusted”?
items.explain: πιστεύσω is future, ἐπίστευον imperfect, πιστεύσας the aorist participle.
items.hook: Augment + stem + σα: ἐπίστευσα.

items.prompt: What does **ἐλύσαμεν** mean?

options.feedback: We were freeing is ἐλύομεν.
You (plural) freed is ἐλύσατε.

items.explain: -σαμεν: the weak aorist “we” ending.
items.hook: -σαμεν = we: ἐλύσαμεν, we freed.
Strong aorist: a new stem with imperfect endings: ἔλαβον, ἔφυγον, ἔμαθον.

items.prompt: λαμβάνω (I take) has the aorist ἔλαβον. What does **ἔλαβε(ν)** mean?

options.feedback: He was taking is ἐλάμβανε(ν), on the present stem.
The augment shows the past.

items.explain: Strong aorist: new stem λαβ- with the imperfect-style endings -ον, -ες, -ε(ν)…
items.hook: λαβ-: a short stem with imperfect-style endings.

items.prompt: How do you tell the imperfect **ἔφευγον** from the aorist **ἔφυγον**?

options.text: By the stem: φευγ- (imperfect) or φυγ- (aorist)
By the ending: the aorist has -σα instead of -ον
options.feedback: Both have -ον, -ες, -ε…: only the stem differs.

options.text: ἔφυγον has no augment; ἔφευγον does
options.feedback: Both have the augment ἐ-.

items.explain: Learn every strong aorist with its stem: φεύγω, ἔφυγον; λαμβάνω, ἔλαβον; μανθάνω, ἔμαθον.
items.hook: φευγ- (imperfect) or φυγ- (aorist): the stem tells you which.

items.prompt: Which is the aorist of **ὁράω** (I see), “I saw”?
items.explain: ὁράω, ἑώρων (I was seeing), ὄψομαι (I will see), εἶδον (I saw), ἰδών (having seen). “Idea” comes from the same root.
items.hook: εἶδον, I saw → **idea**, from the same root.

items.prompt: Which is the aorist of **ἔρχομαι** (I come, go), “I came”?
items.explain: ἔρχομαι, ἦλθον; aorist participle ἐλθών (having come).
items.hook: ἦλθον: a whole new stem, like English go, went.

items.prompt: What does **εἶπον** mean?
items.explain: εἶπον is the aorist of λέγω: I said (or they said).
items.hook: εἶπον shares its root with ἔπος, a word: the source of **epic**.

items.prompt: μανθάνω (I learn) has the aorist ἔμαθον. Which English word shares its root?

options.feedback: Marathon is a place name.
Method comes from μετά + ὁδός (a way after).

items.explain: μάθημα = something learned; μαθηματικός = keen to learn.
items.hook: μαθ- → **mathematics**, things learned.

items.prompt: What does **ἀπέθανε(ν)** (from ἀποθνῄσκω, I die) mean?

options.feedback: He was dying is ἀπέθνῃσκε(ν), on the present stem.
He killed is ἀπέκτεινε(ν), from ἀποκτείνω.

items.explain: ἀποθνῄσκω, ἀπέθανον: a compound, so the augment sits after ἀπο-.
items.hook: θαν- → θάνατος, death.

items.prompt: ἔπαθον is the aorist of πάσχω (I suffer). Which English words are related?

options.feedback: Path is an old English word.
They come (through Italian, French and Latin) from a different Greek word, πάστη (barley porridge), not from πάσχω.

items.explain: πάθος = suffering, feeling. Sympathy = feeling with someone.
items.hook: παθ- → **pathos**, **sympathy**, **empathy**.

items.prompt: **ἠγάγομεν** comes from ἄγω (I lead). What does it mean?

options.feedback: We were leading is ἤγομεν.
The augment (α → η) shows it is past.

items.explain: ἄγω has the strong aorist ἤγαγον, with a doubled stem ἀγαγ-.
items.hook: ἤγαγον: the stem doubles, ἀγ-αγ-.

items.prompt: Which is the aorist of **εὑρίσκω** (I find), “I found”?
items.explain: εὑρίσκω, εὗρον. Archimedes shouted εὕρηκα (eureka), “I have found it!”: that is the perfect tense.
items.hook: εὗρον, I found: the same root as **eureka** (εὕρηκα), I have found it!

items.prompt: **ἔβαλλον** or **ἔβαλον**: which means “I threw” (a single throw)?

options.feedback: ἔβαλλον has the present stem βαλλ-: I was throwing.
The single λ is the aorist stem.

items.explain: βάλλω, ἔβαλον. A “ballistic” missile is a thrown one.
items.hook: One λ for one throw: ἔβαλον.

items.prompt: Which pair are both infinitives?

options.feedback: λύει = he frees; λύσει = he will free.
Those are participles.

items.explain: Present infinitive -ειν; weak aorist infinitive -σαι; strong aorist infinitive -εῖν (λαβεῖν).
items.hook: Three infinitive endings: -ειν (λύειν), -σαι (λῦσαι), -εῖν (λαβεῖν).

items.prompt: What does **ἐθέλω φυγεῖν** mean?

options.feedback: I fled is ἔφυγον.
There is no “them”: the wanter and the fleer are the same person.

items.explain: φυγεῖν is the strong aorist infinitive of φεύγω: to flee (once).
items.hook: φυγεῖν: aorist stem φυγ- + -εῖν.

items.prompt: What does **δεῖ ἡμᾶς μένειν** mean?

options.feedback: Wanting is ἐθέλω.
ἡμᾶς is “us”, the people who must stay.

items.explain: δεῖ + accusative + infinitive: “it is necessary for us to stay”, so “we must stay”.
items.hook: δεῖ + accusative + infinitive = must: δεῖ ἡμᾶς μένειν.

items.prompt: **ὁ βασιλεὺς ἐκέλευσε τοὺς δούλους τὸν ἵππον λῦσαι.** What did the king order?

options.text: the slaves to free the horse
the horse to free the slaves
options.feedback: τοὺς δούλους (accusative) are the people ordered; τὸν ἵππον is the object of λῦσαι.
λῦσαι is active: to free.

items.explain: κελεύω + accusative (the person) + infinitive (the action).
items.hook: κελεύω + accusative (the person) + infinitive (the action).

items.prompt: Which is the aorist infinitive of **λαμβάνω**?

options.feedback: λαμβάνειν is the present infinitive.
ἔλαβον is “I took”, not an infinitive.

items.explain: Strong aorist stem λαβ- + -εῖν: λαβεῖν, to take.
items.hook: λαβ- + -εῖν = λαβεῖν, to take.

items.prompt: What does **φεῦγε** mean?

options.feedback: He flees is φεύγει.
To several people: φεύγετε.

items.explain: Present imperative: φεῦγε (singular), φεύγετε (plural).
items.hook: φεῦγε to one person, φεύγετε to several.

items.prompt: Odysseus shouts **λύσατέ με!** to his crew. What does he mean?

options.text: Untie me! (to more than one person)

options.feedback: λύσατε has no augment, so it is a command. “You untied” is ἐλύσατε.
To one person it would be λῦσόν με; λύσατε is plural.

items.explain: Aorist imperative: λῦσον (singular), λύσατε (plural).
items.hook: No augment = a command: λύσατε!

items.prompt: How do you say “Don’t flee!” to one person?

options.feedback: Commands use μή, not οὐ.
The negative goes first, and with a command it is μή.

items.explain: μή + imperative = “don’t…!”
items.hook: μή + imperative = don’t!

items.prompt: What is the difference between **λύσατε** and **ἐλύσατε**?

options.text: λύσατε is a command; ἐλύσατε is a statement

options.feedback: The augment ἐ- makes it a past statement.

options.text: λύσατε is the future: you will free
options.feedback: The future is λύσετε.

items.explain: No augment on imperatives or infinitives: the augment belongs only to past statements.
items.hook: The augment belongs only to past statements.

items.prompt: What does **ἄκουε** mean?
items.explain: ἄκουε: present imperative of ἀκούω, said to one person.
items.hook: ἄκουε! → **acoustic**: listen!

items.prompt: Which word fills the gap: **ἐθέλομεν τὴν πόλιν ___** (we want to see the city)?

options.feedback: εἶδον = I saw: not an infinitive.
ὁρᾷ = he sees.

items.explain: ἰδεῖν is the strong aorist infinitive of ὁράω: to see.
items.hook: ἰδεῖν: the ἰδ- of **idea**.
ε + ω = ω, ε + ε = ει, ε + ει = ει, ε + ο = ου, ε + ου = ου.

items.prompt: Put the present of φιλέω in order: I, you (sg), he, we, you (pl), they.
items.explain: φιλῶ, φιλεῖς, φιλεῖ, φιλοῦμεν, φιλεῖτε, φιλοῦσι(ν): I love… they love.
items.hook: Chant: φιλῶ, φιλεῖς, φιλεῖ, φιλοῦμεν, φιλεῖτε, φιλοῦσι(ν).

items.prompt: How does φιλέομεν become **φιλοῦμεν**?

options.feedback: It merges with the ο to make ου.
The ου comes from ε + ο.

items.explain: ε + ο = ου; ε + ε = ει; ε + ω = ω.
items.hook: ε + ο = ου.

items.prompt: What does **ποιοῦσι(ν)** mean?

options.feedback: He makes is ποιεῖ.
We make is ποιοῦμεν.

items.explain: ποιέ-ουσι → ποιοῦσι (ε + ου = ου). “Poet” comes from ποιητής, a maker.
items.hook: ποιοῦσι, they make: a poet is a maker.

items.prompt: Which is the infinitive of **φιλέω**?

options.feedback: The ε + ει contracts to ει.
φιλοῦν is the neuter participle.

items.explain: φιλέ-ειν → φιλεῖν, to love.
items.hook: ε + ει = ει: φιλεῖν, to love.

items.prompt: What does **ζητεῖ** (from ζητέω) mean?
items.explain: ζητέω = I seek, look for: ζητεῖ, he or she seeks.
items.hook: ε + ει = ει: ζητεῖ, he seeks.

items.passage:
ὁ Δαίδαλος καὶ ὁ Ἴκαρος

ὁ Δαίδαλος τεχνίτης σοφός ἐστιν. ἐν τῇ Κρήτῃ μένει μετὰ τοῦ Ἰκάρου, τοῦ υἱοῦ. ὁ δὲ Μίνως, ὁ βασιλεύς, οὐκ ἐθέλει αὐτοὺς ἀπολύειν.

ὁ οὖν Δαίδαλος ἐκ κηροῦ καὶ πτερῶν πτέρυγας ποιεῖ. τὸν δὲ υἱὸν κελεύει μὴ ἐγγὺς τοῦ ἡλίου πέτεσθαι. ἔπειτα ὁ πατὴρ καὶ ὁ υἱὸς ἐκ τῆς Κρήτης πέτονται.

ὁ δὲ Ἴκαρος μάλα χαίρει καὶ πρὸς τὸν ἥλιον πέτεται. ὁ οὖν ἥλιος τὸν κηρὸν λύει, καὶ ὁ παῖς εἰς τὴν θάλασσαν πίπτει. ὁ δὲ Δαίδαλος δακρύει.

Glossary: τεχνίτης = craftsman; υἱός = son; ἀπολύειν = to let go; κηρός = wax; πτερόν = feather; πτέρυξ (accusative plural πτέρυγας) = wing; ποιεῖ = makes; κελεύει = orders; μή = not; ἐγγύς (+ genitive) = near; πέτεσθαι = to fly; πέτονται = they fly; πέτεται = he flies; χαίρει = enjoys himself; πίπτει = falls; δακρύει = weeps.
items.passageSource: Adapted for this app from the myth of Daedalus and Icarus
items.hook: τεχνίτης is built on τέχνη, skill: as in technology.

ἡ Ἀράχνη

ἡ Ἀράχνη κόρη ἐστὶν ἐν τῇ Λυδίᾳ. καλῶς ὑφαίνει· πολλοὶ οὖν ἄνθρωποι τὰ ἔργα αὐτῆς θαυμάζουσιν. ἡ δὲ Ἀράχνη λέγει· «ἐγὼ κάλλιον ὑφαίνω ἢ ἡ Ἀθηνᾶ.»

ὁ Ὀρφεὺς μουσικὸς ἄριστος ἦν. ὅτε ᾖδεν, καὶ τὰ δένδρα καὶ τὰ θηρία ἤκουεν. ἡ δὲ γυνὴ αὐτοῦ, ἡ Εὐρυδίκη, ὑπ᾽ ὄφεως δάκνεται καὶ ἀποθνῄσκει.

items.passage:
ὁ Ἰάσων καὶ τὸ χρυσοῦν δέρας

ὁ Πελίας ὁ βασιλεὺς τὸν Ἰάσονα ἐκέλευσε τὸ χρυσοῦν δέρας ἐκ τῆς Κόλχιδος φέρειν. ὁ οὖν Ἰάσων ναῦν μεγάλην, τὴν Ἀργώ, ἐποίησε καὶ μετὰ πολλῶν ἡρώων ἔπλευσεν.

ἐν δὲ τῇ Κόλχιδι ὁ βασιλεὺς Αἰήτης εἶπεν· «εἰ ἐθέλεις τὸ δέρας λαβεῖν, πρῶτον δεῖ σε τοὺς ταύρους ζεῦξαι.» οἱ δὲ ταῦροι πῦρ ἔπνεον.

ἡ δὲ Μήδεια, ἡ τοῦ βασιλέως θυγάτηρ, τὸν Ἰάσονα ἐφίλησε καὶ φάρμακον αὐτῷ ἔδωκεν. τῷ φαρμάκῳ ὁ Ἰάσων τοὺς ταύρους ἔζευξε καὶ τὸ δέρας ἔλαβεν. ἔπειτα μετὰ τῆς Μηδείας ἔφυγεν.

items.passage:
ὁ Περσεὺς καὶ ἡ τῆς Μεδούσης κεφαλή

ὁ Πολυδέκτης ὁ βασιλεὺς τὸν Περσέα ἐκέλευσε τὴν τῆς Μεδούσης κεφαλὴν φέρειν. ὁ δὲ Περσεὺς οὐ φοβούμενος ἐξῆλθεν. ἡ Ἀθηνᾶ καὶ ὁ Ἑρμῆς αὐτῷ ἐβοήθησαν· ἡ μὲν ἀσπίδα λαμπρὰν ἔδωκεν, ὁ δὲ ἅρπην καὶ πτερωτὰ πέδιλα.

ὁ οὖν Περσεὺς πετόμενος πρὸς τὴν τῶν Γοργόνων νῆσον ἦλθεν. τῶν δὲ Γοργόνων καθευδουσῶν, οὐκ εἰς τὴν Μέδουσαν ἀλλ᾽ εἰς τὴν ἀσπίδα βλέπων, τὴν κεφαλὴν αὐτῆς ἀπέτεμεν. ἔπειτα τὴν κεφαλὴν λαβὼν ἀπέφυγεν.

ὕστερον δὲ τῷ Πολυδέκτῃ τὴν κεφαλὴν δείξας, αὐτὸν εἰς λίθον μετέβαλεν.
